name: The Junipers of Kochozenji

location.address: 505 Ayusawa, Minami-Alps City, Yamanashi Prefecture (古長禅寺, 山梨県南アルプス市鮎沢505)

access: Free, temple grounds open daily 9:00-17:00 year-round (境内自由・無休). Public Zen temple courtyard, no appointment needed.
transport: About 40 minutes by bus from Kofu Station
verify_notes: FOUR Chinese junipers (Byakushin), not one: designated together as a single National Natural Monument (国指定天然記念物, designated 1953-11-14) at Kochozenji temple (古長禅寺, Rinzai Myoshin-ji branch), Minami-Alps City, Yamanashi. Planted about 10m apart at the four corners of the former guest hall's front courtyard, said to represent the Four Heavenly Kings (四天王), traditionally attributed to the temple's founder Muso Kokushi at the temple's founding in 1316 (this is the documented planting-date basis for the ~700yr age estimate: 2026-1316=710, sources independently say 'about 700 years'). Girth (measured at 1.5m) ranges 2.00-3.90m across the four trees; height 11.20-17.70m. Nicknamed 'Yotsu-byakudan' / 'four Byakushin'. Two independent official sources agree: Minami-Alps City's own heritage page and the national Agency for Cultural Affairs heritage database (online.bunka.go.jp). Temple founded by Muso Kokushi in 1316; the mother of Takeda Shingen (Oi-fujin) used it as her family temple. Alive evidence: a dated (2019-08-21) CC BY-SA 4.0 photo on Commons shows the northwest and southwest trees standing and green; still listed as a current national monument on the government's own database as of this research (2026-09). Flagged only because the most recent DATED photo I found is from 2019 (7 years old) rather than the last couple of years; the official government registry listing is current, which is reasonably strong but not a same-year photo. TOWN NOTE: this stands in Minami-Alps City, NOT Hokuto -- roughly 20km from the published Jindai-zakura tree in Hokuto (35.780798, 138.367517), too far to be part of that page's walkable cluster. It IS close (~3.6km) to the other candidate in this pass, Mitsue no Okeyaki -- both sit in the Minami-Alps/Kofu-basin area and could form their own small cluster/page rather than joining Hokuto. Commons category gives tree-level coordinates (35.5958,138.4705) matching the brief's coordinate closely, and the temple's own street address (505 Ayusawa) pins it precisely, hence confirmed precision. Collectibility: this is a compact, single-site ensemble (all four trees inside one small temple courtyard, one obvious place to stand), analogous to other approved ensembles, not a scattered avenue.

name: The Great Zelkova of Mitsue

location.address: 1509 Terabe, Minami-Alps City, Yamanashi Prefecture (山梨県南アルプス市寺部1509), on the site of a former shrine, now municipal (city-owned) land

access: Free, no ticket. Stands on municipal land (the site of a former, now-vanished shrine), reached by public residential streets/alleys; OSM shows no private-access restriction on the approach roads. Honest caveat: the lane in is narrow with no dedicated parking, and it sits among houses, so visitors should be quiet and considerate of residents.
transport: About 30 minutes by bus from JR Kofu Station to Nakajo-iriguchi stop, then about 15 minutes on foot; about 10 minutes by car from the Chubu-Odan Expressway's Minami-Alps IC
verify_notes: One of the 'Three Great Zelkovas of Japan' (日本三大ケヤキ, alongside Haramachi's in Gunma and Higashine's in Yamagata) -- genuinely a destination-grade tree, not a park filler. National Natural Monument, designated 1928-11-30 (one of the oldest such designations), on the strength of its size: trunk girth at breast height about 14.2-14.35m per the national Agency for Cultural Affairs database and the city's own page (a separate older source gives 14.7m; treat 14.2-14.35m, the two official figures, as the reliable pair and note the discrepancy), root-level girth about 17.28m, height 20-25m (sources disagree between 20m and 25m; used 25m per the city page, noted the lower figure exists). Estimated age 'over 1,000 years' per both official sources -- a vague age from a real source, kept vague as instructed, not sharpened. Historically stood on a shrine site that no longer exists; the trunk looks split into two from the outside because a lightning-caused fire hollowed and destroyed the tree's central core long ago, but it is one tree, confirmed by the base. In October 2019 Typhoon Hagibis (Typhoon No.19) snapped a major northern limb; the city completed emergency treatment (wound dressing, disinfection, cable bracing of remaining limbs) by February 2020, and a 2020-03-16 local news article (sannichi.lekumo.biz) confirms the tree survived, is under active municipal preservation care, and was already sprouting new growth (hikobae) from the base. That is the most recent dated alive-evidence found (about 6 years old); flagged for that reason, though the government's national-monument listing is still current today (2026) and active local preservation (posts/cabling since 1996) argues for continued care rather than neglect. ACCESS finding worth recording for the writer: one Tripadvisor-adjacent search result described a cramped residential approach with no parking and a sense locals would rather not have tourist traffic; I could not independently verify hostility, but the physical description (narrow lane, no parking) is corroborated by the address being a specific residential plot (寺部1509) surrounded by houses and orchards per Wikipedia. The land itself is confirmed municipal/public (former shrine site, city-owned), not a private garden, so it clears hard rule 10, but the access line should set honest expectations about the approach rather than imply a grand public park. TOWN NOTE: stands in Minami-Alps City (Terabe), same city as Kochozenji (tmpc_001, ~3.6km away) and about 20km from the published Jindai-zakura page in Hokuto -- too far for that page's cluster. Recommend Kochozenji + this tree form their own Minami-Alps City walk/page rather than being folded into Hokuto.
